title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: In an agent, what decides which step comes next in the middle of a request?

options.text: The program's code, which lists every step in order before the request starts
The model, which looks at the results so far and chooses the next action
The student's message, which spells out each step the assistant must take
The tool that ran last, which tells the program which tool to run next

items.stem: Every booking request in your makerspace assistant needs the same three steps in the same order: check the calendar, check the training record, then book. Which design fits best?

options.text: An agent, because it can pick tools freely and so handles bookings more flexibly
An agent, because any request that uses tools needs the model to steer it
A fixed workflow, because the steps are known and the code can run them in order
A fixed workflow, because a model cannot be trusted to call tools in any design

items.stem: A student asks, "My cuts keep burning at the edges; what am I doing wrong?" You cannot know in advance which manuals, settings or follow-up checks the answer will need. Which design fits best?

options.text: An agent, because each next step depends on what the last result showed
A fixed workflow, because every question should follow the same pipeline
A fixed workflow, because an agent cannot search the manuals at all
An agent, because an agent always costs less than a fixed workflow

items.stem: A fixed workflow answers each FAQ question with exactly 2 model calls. An agent doing the same job averages 5 model calls per question, and every call costs the same. For 300 questions, how many more model calls does the agent make than the workflow?
Give one reason, in a short phrase or sentence, why a fixed workflow can be better than an agent for a task whose steps are known in advance.
Your program always runs three steps in this order: the model classifies the question, the model drafts a reply, the model polishes it. Is this an agent?

options.text: Yes, because the model is called at every step of the request
Yes, because three model calls in a row count as a loop
No, because an agent is not allowed to call the model more than once
No, because the code, not the model, fixes the order of the steps
